title: Effects of Popular Science Writing Instruction on General Education Student Attitudes Towards Science: A Case Study in Astronomy
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether popular science writing instruction can improve non-STEM undergraduates’ attitudes toward science, their sense of science’s relevance and benefits, and their confidence in engaging with STEM-related tasks. The authors focus on a gap in prior research: science writing interventions had been studied more often with STEM majors, but less with general education students who are not planning science careers. The study asks how a writing-focused introductory astronomy/astrobiology course affects students’ interest in science, views of scientists, and confidence in reading, explaining, and writing about science.

The intervention was a writing-intensive seminar on astrobiology and science journalism. Students completed scaffolded assignments including summarizing a research paper for a lay audience in Astrobites style, developing a popular science article from idea to full draft, keeping weekly writing journals, reading both technical and non-technical science texts, and participating in class activities on audience, genre, revision, and communication. The course also included discussion of diverse scientists, the nature of science, and science communication. Data were collected through pre/post Google Forms surveys containing Likert-scale items and open-ended questions, plus follow-up interviews with a subset of students.

The population consisted of first-year undergraduates at UCLA, a large public university in the United States, enrolled in a year-long general education “Big Ideas” program; the focal course was the third-quarter seminar. The seminar met once weekly for 2 hours and 50 minutes over 10 weeks, with about 9 hours of outside work each week. The analyzed sample was small: 19 of 21 students from the 2022 offering responded to study assessments, 11 of 21 students from the 2021 offering consented to retrospective use of course evaluations, and 5 students participated in interviews. The study was conducted in a single institutional setting and largely relied on self-reported attitudes and experiences.

The main conclusion is that popular science writing instruction was associated with more positive student attitudes toward science engagement, especially in perceived ability and confidence. Students reported feeling more comfortable reading research papers, more positive about reading science news, more confident explaining science concepts, and more capable of writing about scientific discoveries. They also described writing as a bridge between humanities and STEM, helping them understand science more deeply and see science as relevant to their lives. Interest in astronomy itself changed less, likely because many students already entered with relatively high interest. The authors argue that writing-focused science education can broaden non-majors’ views of how they can participate in science and support scientific literacy and informed citizenship.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-methods/qualitative education study of a writing-intensive astronomy/science journalism course, not an AI intervention study. It uses surveys, interviews, and descriptive statistics with a small sample, so it does not provide causal evidence about an AI tool.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive student attitude and confidence changes from a science writing instructional intervention, but no AI tool is evaluated and no effect sizes are reported. Impact is therefore not applicable to AI tools and remains unclear in the requested framework.
